title: Graphic Design Basics: Become a Graphic Designer
tagline: Learn to see like a designer, use colour and type with confidence, then build logos, layouts and a portfolio that wins clients.
takeaways: Build grids for posts and print
description:
Graphic design is a skill, not a gift. Designers follow clear ideas that anyone can learn, and those ideas work in every app. This course teaches design itself, not one tool, and shows you the path to working as a graphic designer.

**Basic stages (free):**

- **How designers see:** hierarchy, contrast, alignment, proximity, repetition and white space.
- **Colour:** the colour wheel, simple palettes, contrast for readability, and RGB versus CMYK in plain words.
- **Typography:** choosing and pairing fonts, sizes, and readable text in English and Urdu.

**Advanced stages (Premium):**

- **Layout and grids:** social posts, banners and print pieces that are built on a clear structure.
- **Logos and brand identity:** vector logos, logo versions and a simple brand guide.
- **Working as a designer:** briefs, revisions, file formats, copyright and licences, a portfolio and pricing your work.

You can practise with free or paid editors, such as Figma, GIMP, Inkscape, Photopea or Adobe apps. Menus and plans change, so the course teaches ideas you can use in any version. Follow Mahnoor, a student in Karachi, from her first messy flyer to her first brand project for a café in Islamabad.
audience: Students and fresh graduates who want to start a career in graphic design
Freelancers who already make designs and want to understand why some work and others do not
Small-business owners and marketing staff who brief designers or make their own materials
Print shop and advertising staff who prepare files for customers
Anyone who uses a design app but feels unsure about layout, colour and fonts
outcomes: Use hierarchy, contrast, alignment, proximity, repetition and white space to make clear designs
Build colour palettes with readable contrast and explain RGB and CMYK in plain words
Choose, pair and size fonts for readable English and Urdu text
Set up grids, margins and safe areas for social posts, banners and print
Design a simple vector logo with versions and a one-page brand guide
Work with clients using briefs, agreed revisions, correct files and honest pricing
Build a portfolio and respect copyright and licences for fonts and images

sessions.title: How Designers See: Hierarchy, Contrast, Alignment and Space
sessions.summary: Learn the six ideas designers use to guide the eye: hierarchy, contrast, alignment, proximity, repetition and white space. You will spot why a flyer feels messy and fix it step by step, in any design app.
objectives: Explain hierarchy, contrast, alignment, proximity, repetition and white space in plain words
Plan the order in which people should notice things on a design
Use alignment and proximity to group information clearly
Use white space on purpose instead of filling every corner
Test a design quickly with the squint test and the phone test

cards.title: The flyer nobody read
cards.setting: An online mentoring call. Mahnoor is in Karachi, Nida in Lahore and Danish in Peshawar.

lines.text: Welcome to The Designer's Sketchbook. Your first page begins with a flyer that tried to say everything at once.
I made this flyer for my cousin's tuition centre. It has the subjects, the fees, three phone numbers, a map, five photos and a quote. People take it and still call to ask what it is!
Honestly, my eyes jump around. I cannot tell where to start reading.
That is the key point. Before colours or fonts, a designer decides what people should see first, second and third. A design is a path for the eye.
So I should decide the order before I touch the app?
Exactly. Six simple ideas will fix this flyer, and they work in any software you ever use. Let us learn to see like designers.

scenes.heading: Hierarchy
scenes.narration: Hierarchy is the order of importance. The most important message is the biggest or boldest, so the eye knows where to start.

scenes.heading: Contrast
scenes.narration: Contrast is a clear difference: big and small, dark and light, bold and thin. Without contrast, everything looks the same and nothing stands out.

scenes.heading: Alignment
scenes.narration: Alignment means lining things up along shared edges or a centre line. It makes a page look planned, even when the viewer cannot say why.

scenes.heading: Proximity
scenes.narration: Proximity means keeping related things close together, like a course name and its timing. Unrelated things get more space between them.

scenes.heading: Repetition
scenes.narration: Repetition means using the same colours, fonts and shapes again and again, so the design feels like one family.

scenes.heading: White space
scenes.narration: White space is the empty space around and between things. It is not wasted. It gives the important parts room to breathe.

cards.title: Plan the reading order
cards.caption: Decide this order on paper first. Then make each step a little less loud than the one before.

items.label: 1. Main message
items.detail: The one idea people must notice first, such as 'Maths and Science Classes'.

items.label: 2. Supporting image
items.detail: One clear picture or shape that supports the message.

items.label: 3. Key detail
items.detail: The reason to act, such as 'New batch starts 1 March'.

items.label: 4. Action
items.detail: What to do next: call, visit or scan, shown once and clearly.

items.label: 5. Small print
items.detail: Address, timings and social handle, smaller and quieter.

cards.question: Mahnoor's flyer shows subjects, fees, three phone numbers, a map and five photos at about the same size. What should she decide first?
options: Which bright colour to use for the background
The one main message people must notice first
A new font that looks more modern
How to fit in one more photo
cards.explanation: When everything is the same size, nothing leads. Choosing the main message first gives the design a clear starting point. Colour and fonts come after the order of importance is set.

cards.title: Contrast is more than colour
cards.body:
Many beginners think contrast only means bright colours. Designers create contrast in several ways:

- **Size:** a big headline against small details.
- **Weight:** bold text against regular text.
- **Colour and tone:** dark against light, or one bright accent on a calm background.
- **Shape:** one round shape among square ones.
- **Space:** one item with lots of room around it.

Use contrast for the few things that matter. If everything is big, bold and bright, there is no contrast left, and the page shouts without saying anything.

cards.back: Showing what is most important first, then second, then third.
Making differences clear, so important things stand out from the rest.
Lining items up along the same edge or centre so the page looks organised.
Keeping related items close and unrelated items apart, so groups are easy to see.
Reusing colours, fonts and shapes so the design feels consistent.
Empty space that separates groups and draws attention to the main message.

cards.title: The tuition flyer: before and after
cards.caption: Same information, far clearer. Only the design ideas changed.

items.label: Focus
items.left: Everything the same size; no clear start
items.right: One headline, clearly the biggest

items.label: Grouping
items.left: Fees, phone and map scattered around
items.right: Contact details grouped together at the bottom

items.label: Alignment
items.left: Text centred, left and right at random
items.right: All text lined up on one left edge

items.label: Photos
items.left: Five small photos fighting for attention
items.right: One strong photo of students learning

items.label: Space
items.right: Clear margins and space between groups

cards.title: Fill the empty space?
cards.situation: Mahnoor shows the new flyer to her cousin, who owns the tuition centre. He says: 'It looks nice, but there is so much empty space. Can you add our other branches, the teachers' photos and a few student quotes there?'

choices.text: Explain that the space helps the main offer stand out, and suggest putting the extra details on the back or a social post.
choices.outcome: Her cousin agrees once he sees the flyer is easier to read from a distance. The extra content goes on the back. The front stays clear and works better.

choices.text: Add just the branch list in small text at the bottom and keep the rest of the space.
choices.outcome: A fair compromise. The flyer gets a little busier but still has a clear focus. It is acceptable, though a back side would have kept it cleaner.

choices.text: Add everything he asked for, because the client is always right.
choices.outcome: The flyer is crowded again and loses its main message. Clients value designers who explain their choices kindly and offer a better solution.

cards.title: Which principle is at work?
cards.prompt: Sort each design choice under the principle it mainly uses.

items.text: Every text box starts from the same left edge
The phone number sits right next to the 'Call now' line
All headings use the same font and colour
The logo is centred above a centred headline
Each product name is placed directly above its price
The same round icon style is used for every feature
Social handles are grouped together in one corner
Every post in a series has the same coloured strip at the top

cards.title: Contrast and order together
cards.caption: A strong design needs both clear contrast and a neat, aligned structure.

items.label: Tidy but dull
items.detail: Neat and aligned, but nothing stands out, so it is easy to ignore.

items.label: Clear and professional
items.detail: Neat structure with one strong focus. This is the goal.

items.label: Lost in the noise
items.detail: Messy and flat. The eye has nothing to hold on to.

items.label: Loud but confusing
items.detail: Bold elements everywhere, placed at random. It shouts but says little.

cards.question: On a menu, the dish names are far from their prices and the prices sit in a separate column on the other side of the page. Which principle would fix this most directly?
options: Repetition
White space
Proximity
Hierarchy
cards.explanation: Proximity says related things belong close together. Putting each price next to its dish makes them read as one unit, so customers do not have to match them up.

cards.title: Danish fixes a mobile shop poster
cards.body:
Danish's friend runs a fictional mobile repair shop, Fix-It Corner, in Peshawar. The old poster had eight services in eight colours.

- **Hierarchy:** 'Screen repair in 1 hour' became the headline, the shop's main selling point.
- **Proximity:** the other services went into one short list, grouped together.
- **Alignment:** everything was lined up on the left edge.
- **Repetition:** one accent colour was used for the headline and the 'Visit us' line only.
- **White space:** the margins were doubled.

The shop owner said customers now read the poster from across the road.

cards.title: Two quick tests
cards.body:
**The squint test:** half-close your eyes and look at your design. The thing you still see clearly should be your main message. If several things compete, reduce some of them.

**The phone test:** most people see designs on a phone. Shrink your design to phone size, or send it to yourself, and check that the main message is still readable in two or three seconds.

cards.title: Problem and fix
cards.prompt: Match each design problem with the principle that fixes it.

pairs.right: Contrast: make the main message clearly different

pairs.left: Text boxes start at random places
pairs.right: Alignment: line items up along a shared edge
Proximity: group related details together

pairs.left: Each page of a booklet looks different
pairs.right: Repetition: reuse the same fonts, colours and shapes
White space: give groups room to breathe

cards.title: Remember from The First Sketch
items: Decide the reading order on paper before you open any app.
Hierarchy and contrast make one message the clear winner.
Alignment and proximity turn scattered items into tidy groups.
Repetition makes a design, or a series of designs, feel like one family.
White space is a tool, not wasted space.
Check every design with the squint test and the phone test.

cards.prompt: Find a poster, flyer or social post near you that feels messy. Write down what it should say first, second and third, and which two principles would fix it most.

quiz.question: What does 'hierarchy' mean in graphic design?
options: Using as many bright colours as possible on one page
The order of importance shown on a design
The name of the main font
The size of the printed paper
quiz.explanation: Hierarchy is the order of importance. It tells the viewer what to look at first, second and third.

quiz.question: A poster's headline, photo and price are all huge, bold and red. What is the main problem?
options: The paper is too small
The photo is not colourful or large enough to attract people
There are not enough fonts
Too many things compete, so nothing leads
quiz.explanation: When several items use every kind of emphasis, none of them stands out. Pick one winner and tone down the rest.

quiz.question: Which choice shows proximity used well?
options: Each phone number sits next to its branch
Every heading uses a different font
All text is centred on the page
The logo is the largest item on the page, above everything else
quiz.explanation: Proximity keeps related items together, so the viewer sees them as one group.

quiz.question: Why do designers leave white space on a page?
options: To save printing ink
Because clients usually prefer pages with very little on them
To separate groups and focus attention
To make the file smaller
quiz.explanation: White space separates groups and focuses attention. It makes a design look calm and confident.

quiz.question: Which of these is a way to create contrast besides colour?
options: Using the same size for all text
A big headline next to small details
Placing every item in the centre
Adding more photos of the same size
quiz.explanation: Size is a strong way to create contrast. Weight, shape and space can create contrast too.

quiz.question: A set of five social posts uses the same two fonts, one accent colour and the same strip at the top. Which principle is this mainly using?
options: White space
Alignment
Hierarchy
Repetition
quiz.explanation: Repeating fonts, colours and shapes across designs makes them feel like one consistent family.

quiz.question: What is the squint test for?
options: Seeing what still stands out when details blur
Checking the spelling of small text
Measuring the size of the margins
Checking whether small text is spelled correctly before printing
quiz.explanation: When you half-close your eyes, details blur and only strong elements remain. Your main message should be one of them.

quiz.question: Mahnoor's text boxes start at different distances from the left edge. Which principle is she breaking?
options: Repetition
Contrast
Alignment
White space
quiz.explanation: Alignment lines items up along shared edges. Random starting points make a page look unplanned.

quiz.question: A client asks you to fill all the empty space on a clear flyer with extra text. What is the most professional response?
options: Refuse to change anything
Explain why the space helps and offer another place for the text
Add everything quietly without comment
Make all the text smaller so that everything he asked for fits on the front
quiz.explanation: Good designers explain their choices kindly and offer solutions, such as a back side or a separate post, so the main message stays clear.

quiz.question: Why should you check a design at phone size?
options: Phones print designs differently
Phone screens always show more colours than laptops or printed paper
Apps refuse large files
Many people first see designs on phones
quiz.explanation: Many viewers see designs on phones, so the main message must still be clear at a small size.

sessions.title: Colour: The Colour Wheel, Palettes and Readable Contrast
sessions.summary: Learn how colours relate on the colour wheel, build small palettes that look planned, keep text readable with strong contrast, and understand in plain words why screen colours (RGB) and print colours (CMYK) can look different.
objectives: Use the colour wheel to find complementary and analogous colours
Build a small palette with main, supporting and accent colours
Check that text has enough contrast to read easily
Explain the difference between RGB for screens and CMYK for print in plain words
Avoid relying on colour alone to carry important information

cards.title: The green that turned grey
cards.setting: Tariq's printing press in Faisalabad, on a video call with Danish in Peshawar.

lines.text: Page two of the sketchbook. Danish has designed a poster for his brother's juice shop, and the printed copy has just come out of the machine.
Tariq uncle, on my laptop the green was so bright and fresh. On paper it looks dull, almost grey!
Beta, I see this every week. Screens make colour with light. My machines make colour with ink. Some bright screen colours cannot be printed exactly.
This is the RGB and CMYK difference, Danish. And I also notice your yellow text on a white background. Can anyone read it from the road?
Not really. I just liked the colours together.
Colour is not only about liking. It must set the mood and keep text readable. Let us build a palette with a plan.

scenes.heading: Primary colours
scenes.narration: In the traditional painter's wheel, red, yellow and blue are the primary colours. Mixing them gives the other colours on the wheel.

scenes.heading: Secondary colours
scenes.narration: Orange, green and violet sit between the primaries. Each is a mix of the two primaries beside it.

scenes.heading: Complementary
scenes.narration: Colours opposite each other on the wheel, like blue and orange, are complementary. Together they create strong contrast and energy.

scenes.heading: Analogous
scenes.narration: Colours side by side on the wheel, like yellow, yellow-green and green, are analogous. They feel calm and natural together.

scenes.heading: Triadic
scenes.narration: Three colours evenly spaced around the wheel form a triad. It is lively, so let one colour lead and use the others lightly.

cards.title: The basic colour wheel
cards.caption: Opposite colours are complementary. Neighbours are analogous.

items.label: Red
items.detail: Opposite green. Energy, urgency, celebration.

items.label: Orange
items.detail: Opposite blue. Warm, friendly, appetising.

items.label: Yellow
items.detail: Opposite violet. Bright and cheerful, but weak as text on white.

items.label: Green
items.detail: Opposite red. Fresh, natural, growth.

items.label: Blue
items.detail: Opposite orange. Calm, trust, cool.

items.label: Violet
items.detail: Opposite yellow. Creative, rich, special.

cards.question: Danish wants a juice shop poster with strong, energetic contrast. Which pair is complementary?
options: Yellow and yellow-green
Blue and orange
Green and blue-green
Red and red-orange
cards.explanation: Blue and orange sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, so they are complementary and create strong contrast. The other pairs are neighbours, which are analogous.

cards.title: A simple palette plan
cards.body:
A palette is the small set of colours you choose and stick to. A popular guideline is **60-30-10**:

- **About 60%:** a main colour, often a calm background.
- **About 30%:** a supporting colour for shapes, panels or headings.
- **About 10%:** an accent colour for the one thing you want noticed, such as a button or offer.

It is a guide, not a law. The point is that one colour leads, one supports and one highlights. Save your palette as colour codes (for example HEX codes like #1D3557) so you can use exactly the same colours every time.

cards.back: The basic colour family, such as red, blue or green.
A colour mixed with white, so it becomes lighter, like pink from red.
A colour mixed with black, so it becomes darker, like maroon from red.
How strong or pure a colour is. Low saturation looks greyish and soft.
A six-character code like #FF5733 that names an exact screen colour.
A small amount of a bold colour used to highlight the most important thing.

cards.title: RGB and CMYK in plain words
cards.caption: Design in the colour mode that matches where the work will end up, and ask your printer what they need.

items.label: Stands for
items.right: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Key (black)

items.label: Made with
items.right: Ink on paper

items.label: Used for
items.right: Flyers, cards, banners, packaging

items.label: Mixing
items.left: More light makes colours brighter, towards white
items.right: More ink makes colours darker

items.label: Watch out
items.left: Very bright screen colours may not print the same
items.right: Ask for a test print of important colours

cards.title: Red on green
cards.situation: A fictional sweets shop in Karachi asks Mahnoor for a sale post with bright red text on a bright green background, 'because those are our shop colours'. When she tries it, the text seems to vibrate and is tiring to read.

choices.text: Keep both brand colours, but put the text in white or a very dark colour on a calm panel, and use red and green as shapes around it.
choices.outcome: The post still feels like the shop's brand, and now the sale is easy to read. The client is happy because their colours are still there.

choices.text: Make the red text bigger and bolder on the same green.
choices.outcome: It is a bit easier to read, but the clash is still tiring. Size helps, but it does not fix weak contrast between two strong colours.

choices.text: Use the colours as asked because the client chose them.
choices.outcome: People scroll past because the text is hard to read. A designer's job is to keep the brand while making the message work.

cards.title: Easy or hard to read?
cards.prompt: Sort each text and background pair by how easy it is to read.

items.text: Black text on a white background
Yellow text on a white background
White text on a dark navy background
Light grey text on a light blue background
Bright red text on a bright green background
Dark brown text on a cream background
White text on a busy photo with no dark overlay
White text on a dark overlay over a photo

cards.title: Contrast ratios to know
cards.caption: Contrast checkers compare text and background. These levels come from the widely used Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG), level AA.

items.label: Normal body text
items.detail: Minimum contrast for regular-sized text.

items.label: Large text
items.detail: Minimum for large or bold headings.

items.label: Black on white
items.detail: The highest contrast possible.

items.label: Same colour on same colour
items.detail: No contrast at all: invisible text.

cards.question: Danish is preparing a flyer for print at Tariq's press. Which colour mode should the final print file use, unless the printer asks otherwise?
options: RGB, because it has brighter colours
CMYK, because printing uses ink
Grayscale, because printers prefer it
Any mode, because it makes no difference
cards.explanation: Print uses cyan, magenta, yellow and black inks, so print files are usually prepared in CMYK. Always confirm with the printer, since some printers prefer to convert files themselves.

cards.title: A palette for the juice shop
cards.body:
Danish rebuilds the poster for the fictional Fresh Press juice shop in Peshawar.

- **Main (about 60%):** a soft cream background, calm and clean.
- **Supporting (about 30%):** a deep green for headings and the fruit panel.
- **Accent (about 10%):** orange, the complement of blue-green, used only on 'Fresh mango juice Rs 250'.

He checks the green text on cream with a free online contrast checker, and it passes for normal text. He saves all three HEX codes in a note and asks Tariq for a small test print before printing a hundred copies.

cards.title: Do not rely on colour alone
cards.body: Some people have colour vision deficiency and may not tell red from green. Colours also carry different meanings in different cultures and contexts. So do not use colour as the only signal: add words, icons or underlines too. A quick test is to view your design in grayscale. If the important parts still stand out, your contrast is working.

cards.title: Build a palette step by step
cards.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order when choosing colours for a new design.
steps: Decide the mood the design should create, such as fresh, calm or festive
Pick one main colour that fits that mood and any brand colours
Use the colour wheel to choose a supporting colour and an accent
Check text and background pairs with a contrast checker
View the design in grayscale and on a phone
Save the colour codes so you can reuse the exact colours

cards.title: Remember from The Paint Box
items: Complementary colours sit opposite on the wheel and create strong contrast.
Analogous colours sit side by side and feel calm together.
Use a small palette: one main colour, one supporting colour and one accent.
Readable contrast matters more than favourite colours.
RGB is light for screens; CMYK is ink for print. Ask your printer what they need.
Never let colour be the only way important information is shown.

cards.prompt: Choose a local business you know. Write a three-colour palette for it (main, supporting and accent), say what mood each colour gives, and explain where you would use the accent.

quiz.question: Which two colours are complementary on the basic colour wheel?
options: Red and orange
Blue and green
Yellow and violet
Green and yellow
quiz.explanation: Complementary colours sit opposite each other. Yellow is opposite violet; the other pairs are neighbours.

quiz.question: What are analogous colours?
options: Colours that sit next to each other on the wheel
Colours that sit directly opposite each other on the colour wheel
Only black, white and grey
Colours used only in print
quiz.explanation: Analogous colours are neighbours on the colour wheel, such as yellow, yellow-green and green. They feel calm together.

quiz.question: In the 60-30-10 guideline, what is the 10% colour usually used for?
options: The whole background
All the body text
The colour of the paper or screen the design is shown on
An accent for the most important thing
quiz.explanation: The small accent share draws attention to the key item, such as an offer or a button.

quiz.question: Why can a bright green on screen look duller when printed?
options: The printer used the wrong paper size and the colours spread out across the page while printing
Screens use light, print uses ink, and some colours cannot be matched
The design file had too many pages
Printed colours are always grey
quiz.explanation: RGB screens mix light, while CMYK printing mixes inks. Some very bright screen colours fall outside what ink can reproduce.

quiz.question: Which text and background pair is hardest to read?
options: Black text on white
White text on dark navy
Dark brown text on cream
Yellow text on white
quiz.explanation: Yellow and white are both very light, so the contrast is too low to read easily.

quiz.question: What does adding white to a colour create?
options: A tint
A shade
A complement
A HEX code
quiz.explanation: A tint is a colour mixed with white, so it becomes lighter. A shade is mixed with black.

quiz.question: A contrast checker shows your body text at 3:1 against its background. Under the common WCAG AA guide, what should you do?
options: Nothing, because 3:1 already passes for body text of any size
Raise it to at least 4.5:1 for normal text
Use a lighter text colour
Add more colours to the text
quiz.explanation: WCAG AA asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text; 3:1 is the minimum only for large text.

quiz.question: Why should colour not be the only way to show important information?
options: Colours cost extra to print
Some people cannot tell certain colours apart
Design apps cannot show red and green together in the same file
Designers must use only one colour
quiz.explanation: People with colour vision deficiency may miss colour-only signals, so add words, icons or other cues.

quiz.question: A client's brand colours are bright red and bright green, and red text on green is hard to read. What is the best approach?
options: Remove both brand colours completely
Use the colours exactly as requested for the text
Keep the colours in shapes, and set text in white or a dark colour on a calm area
Print the design in black and white only
quiz.explanation: This keeps the brand recognisable while making the text readable through strong contrast.

quiz.question: Why should you save a palette as colour codes such as HEX values?
options: Codes make the file print faster and use less ink on every page
So you can reuse exactly the same colours
Codes make colours brighter
Apps require codes before saving
quiz.explanation: Saving exact codes keeps colours consistent across designs, people and apps.

sessions.title: Typography: Choosing, Pairing and Sizing Fonts in English and Urdu
sessions.summary: Learn the basic families of fonts, pair a heading font with a body font, set sizes and spacing that read well, and handle English and Urdu text with care, including right-to-left direction and Nastaliq script.
objectives: Tell serif, sans-serif, script and display fonts apart and choose them for the job
Pair two fonts with clear contrast and a shared mood
Set readable sizes, line spacing and line lengths
Prepare Urdu text that reads right to left and joins correctly
Build a simple type hierarchy for headings, body text and captions

cards.title: Broken letters
cards.setting: Mahnoor's home in Karachi, the night before a school prize day.

lines.text: Page three. Mahnoor is making a bilingual banner in English and Urdu for her old school's prize day.
Nida apa, something is wrong. I pasted the Urdu heading, but the letters are not joining. They appear separate, and the words look backwards!
That usually means the app or the font does not fully support Urdu. Urdu letters change shape and join, and the text runs right to left. Not every program handles that well.
Also, I used four fancy fonts in English because they looked pretty.
Pretty is fine for one word. For reading, you need clarity. Two fonts, good sizes and enough spacing will do more than four decorations.
Teach me, please. The banner goes to print tomorrow at noon!
Then let us start with what fonts are for. Words are the message. Typography is how the message speaks.

scenes.heading: Serif
scenes.narration: Serif fonts have small strokes at the ends of letters. They often feel traditional, formal or bookish.

scenes.heading: Sans-serif
scenes.narration: Sans-serif fonts have clean ends with no strokes. They often feel modern and simple, and they read well on screens.

scenes.heading: Script
scenes.narration: Script fonts look like handwriting. They suit invitations and short words, but long lines in script are hard to read.

scenes.heading: Display
scenes.narration: Display fonts are bold or decorative, made for big headlines. Use them for a few words, never for paragraphs.

scenes.heading: Spacing
scenes.narration: Line spacing, letter spacing and line length matter as much as the font. Good spacing makes ordinary fonts look professional.

cards.title: A simple type hierarchy
cards.caption: Each level is clearly smaller or lighter than the one above it.

items.label: Headline
items.detail: Largest and boldest. A few words only.

items.label: Subheading
items.detail: Smaller, may use the heading font in a lighter weight.

items.label: Body text
items.detail: Comfortable reading size in a plain, readable font.

items.label: Caption and small print
items.detail: Smallest, but still readable: dates, credits, terms.

cards.question: Mahnoor wants a font for a full paragraph of event instructions on a phone screen. Which is usually the best choice?
options: A thin script font that looks like handwriting
A decorative display font with heavy shadows
A clear sans-serif font at a comfortable size
Four different fonts so the paragraph looks lively
cards.explanation: Clean sans-serif fonts at a comfortable size usually read well on screens. Script and display fonts are best kept for a few words.

cards.title: Pairing fonts that work together
cards.body:
Most designs need only **two fonts**: one for headings and one for body text. To pair them well:

- **Create clear contrast:** for example, a bold serif heading with a simple sans-serif body. Two fonts that are almost the same look like a mistake.
- **Share a mood:** both should suit the message, such as friendly, formal or playful.
- **Use a font family:** one family with several weights (light, regular, bold) can give you contrast with no pairing risk.
- **Keep the body font plain:** it does the hard work of being read.

In Urdu designs, pair one clear Urdu font with your English fonts, and match their size and weight so neither language looks like an afterthought.

cards.title: Type words
cards.prompt: Match each typography term with its meaning.

pairs.right: The space between lines of text
The overall spacing between all letters in a word or line
Adjusting the space between two particular letters
How thick or thin the strokes of a font are, such as light or bold
A group of related fonts in several weights and styles
How many characters fit on one line before it wraps

cards.title: Setting English and Urdu text
cards.caption: Bilingual designs look professional when both languages get equal care.

items.label: Direction
items.right: Right to left

items.label: Alignment
items.left: Usually aligned left for body text
items.right: Usually aligned right for body text

items.label: Common style
items.right: Nastaliq for a traditional look; Naskh-style fonts are more upright

items.label: Line spacing
items.right: Nastaliq needs extra line spacing so letters do not touch

items.label: Size
items.left: Set at your normal reading size
items.right: Often needs a larger size to look equal to English

cards.title: The Urdu heading will not join
cards.situation: It is late at night and Mahnoor's Urdu heading appears as separate, backwards letters in her design app. The banner goes to print tomorrow. Danish suggests typing the Urdu in a phone app, taking a screenshot and pasting it onto the banner.

choices.text: Try a font and app known to support Urdu, check the joining with a native reader, and only use a high-resolution image of the text as a last resort.
choices.outcome: She switches to a well-supported Urdu font and the letters join correctly. Her mother reads it back to confirm. The banner prints sharp and correct.

choices.text: Export the Urdu text as a high-resolution image from an app that renders it correctly.
choices.outcome: It works for this banner, but the text is harder to edit later. Acceptable in a rush, as long as the resolution is high enough for print.

choices.text: Use the phone screenshot, since it looks fine on the screen.
choices.outcome: A small screenshot looks blurry and pixelated when printed large on a banner. Never use low-resolution screenshots for print.

cards.title: Readable or not?
cards.prompt: Sort each type choice by its effect on readability.

items.text: A long paragraph written in all capital letters
Body text in a plain font with comfortable line spacing
Lines so long that they run across a wide banner
Urdu Nastaliq text with extra space between lines
Text stretched or squashed to fit a box
One heading font and one body font
Script font used for a full page of rules
Headings clearly larger than body text

cards.question: Mahnoor's Urdu lines in Nastaliq look crowded, with letters from one line touching the next. What should she change first?
options: Increase the line spacing
Switch the Urdu text to all capital letters
Stretch the text horizontally
Make the Urdu much smaller than the English
cards.explanation: Nastaliq letters rise and fall at angles, so they need more line spacing than many English fonts. Urdu has no capital letters, and stretching text distorts it.

cards.title: The prize day banner, fixed
cards.body:
Mahnoor's final banner for the fictional Green Valley School:

- **Headline:** the Urdu title in a clear Nastaliq font on the right, the English title in a bold sans-serif on the left, at sizes that look equal.
- **Body:** date, time and venue in one plain sans-serif, aligned left in English and right in Urdu.
- **Spacing:** extra line spacing for the Urdu lines.
- **Fonts:** two English weights from one family plus one Urdu font, all with licences that allow this use.

She proofreads both languages, asks her mother to read the Urdu aloud, and sends a PDF to the printer.

cards.title: Sizes that read well
cards.body:
There is no single perfect size, because it depends on the font and how far away people are. Some general guides:

- **Phone screens:** if you have to zoom in to read it, it is too small.
- **Printed flyers:** body text is often set somewhere around 9 to 12 points, depending on the font.
- **Banners and signs:** the further away people stand, the bigger the letters and the fewer the words.

Print a test page or view it at real size before you finish.

cards.title: Setting type on a poster
cards.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order when setting the text on a poster.
steps: Write and shorten the text before designing
Mark the headline, subheading, body and small print
Choose a heading font and a body font with clear contrast
Set sizes so each level is clearly different
Adjust line spacing and alignment for each language
Proofread every word, numbers and spellings included

cards.title: Remember from The Letter Press
items: Choose fonts for their job: script and display for a few words, plain fonts for reading.
Two fonts, or one family with several weights, is usually enough.
Make each level of the type hierarchy clearly different in size or weight.
Never stretch or squash text; use a different size or weight instead.
Urdu runs right to left, needs proper font support and extra line spacing for Nastaliq.
Proofread both languages, ideally with a native reader.

cards.prompt: Pick a heading font and a body font you could use for a bilingual English and Urdu event poster. Explain why they work together and how you would make both languages look equally important.

quiz.question: What is a serif?
options: A small stroke at the end of a letter
A type of paper
The space left between two lines of text in a paragraph
A font made only for Urdu
quiz.explanation: Serifs are small strokes at the ends of letters. Fonts without them are called sans-serif.

quiz.question: How many fonts does a typical simple design need?
options: At least five, for variety
Usually two: one for headings, one for body
One new font for each line
None, because all the text should be turned into images first
quiz.explanation: Two fonts, or one family with several weights, usually give enough contrast while keeping the design consistent.

quiz.question: What does 'leading' mean?
options: The first word of a paragraph, set in a larger size
The heaviest weight of a font
The space between lines of text
The colour of the headline
quiz.explanation: Leading, also called line spacing, is the vertical space between lines of text.

quiz.question: Why is a script font a poor choice for a long paragraph?
options: Script fonts cannot be printed
Script fonts only work in Urdu
Script fonts are always too large to fit a paragraph on one page
Handwriting styles tire the eye in long lines
quiz.explanation: Script fonts are fine for a few words but tiring to read in paragraphs, especially at small sizes.

quiz.question: In which direction is Urdu text read?
options: Right to left
Left to right
Top to bottom only
It depends on the font size
quiz.explanation: Urdu is written and read right to left, so body text is usually aligned right.

quiz.question: Urdu letters appear separate and in the wrong order in a design app. What is the most likely cause?
options: The text is too large
The app or font does not fully support Urdu
The colour is not dark enough
The page has too much white space around the Urdu heading
quiz.explanation: Urdu letters change shape and join. Software or fonts without proper support can show them broken or reversed.

quiz.question: Which pairing gives the clearest contrast?
options: Two sans-serif fonts that look almost exactly the same as each other
Two different script fonts
A bold serif heading with a plain sans-serif body
The same font at the same size and weight
quiz.explanation: Pairs need clear contrast. Two fonts that are nearly the same look like a mistake.

quiz.question: A headline does not fit its box. What should you do instead of stretching or squashing it?
options: Stretch it anyway; nobody notices
Change the size, weight or wording, or resize the box
Turn it into a low-resolution screenshot
Add letter spacing until it fills the box
quiz.explanation: Stretching distorts letter shapes. Change the size, weight or words, or adjust the layout.

quiz.question: Why does Nastaliq text often need extra line spacing?
options: Its letters slope and stack, so lines can touch
It uses capital letters
It is always printed in red
It reads from top to bottom, so it needs room above and below every line
quiz.explanation: Nastaliq letters slope and stack, which takes more vertical room than many English fonts.

quiz.question: What is the best final check for a bilingual English and Urdu banner?
options: Check only the English text
Make the Urdu smaller so the English stands out more clearly on the banner
Proofread both languages with a native reader
Print it and fix mistakes later
quiz.explanation: Mistakes are costly once printed. Checking both languages, with a native reader for Urdu, catches joining and spelling errors.

sessions.title: Layout and Grids for Social Posts, Banners and Print
sessions.summary: Step up to professional layout. Build designs on grids with margins, columns and gutters, plan for safe areas, bleed and resolution, and adapt one idea into a social post, a shop banner and a printed flyer without losing its clarity.
objectives: Set up a grid with margins, columns and gutters for any format
Keep important content inside safe areas and add bleed for print
Choose sizes, resolution and colour mode for screen and print
Adapt one design idea to square, tall and wide formats
Prepare a print-ready file and check it with the printer

cards.title: Cut off at the edge
cards.setting: Tariq's printing press in Faisalabad. A customer's banner has just been trimmed.

lines.text: Welcome to the Advanced stages. In the Grid Room, the sketchbook gets serious: real formats, real printers and real deadlines.
Look at this, Danish. The customer's phone number was right at the edge of the design. After trimming, half the last digit is gone. Now he wants a free reprint!
Was it the machine's fault?
No, beta. Every trim can move slightly. Designers must keep important things away from the edge and extend the background past it. That extra is called bleed.
This is where grids help. A grid gives you margins, columns and safe areas, so every element has a planned home.
So a grid is like the lines in a school copy that keep writing straight?
Exactly. Invisible lines, but the viewer feels the order. Professionals rarely design without one.

scenes.heading: Margins
scenes.narration: Margins are the empty borders around the edge of the page. They keep content away from the trim and give the design a calm frame.

scenes.heading: Columns
scenes.narration: Columns are vertical sections that hold text and images. Many layouts use two, three, four or twelve columns, depending on size.

scenes.heading: Gutters
scenes.narration: Gutters are the gaps between columns. Keeping them equal makes the layout feel even and tidy.

scenes.heading: Rows and modules
scenes.narration: Adding horizontal rows creates boxes called modules. Images and text blocks can span one or several modules.

scenes.heading: Safe area
scenes.narration: The safe area is where important content must stay, such as away from the trim in print or from buttons and captions that cover parts of a post on some apps.

cards.title: Setting up a layout grid
cards.caption: Most design apps let you add guides, margins or layout grids. The menu names vary between apps and versions.

items.label: 1. Set the size
items.detail: Choose the final size and units: pixels for screens, millimetres or inches for print.

items.label: 2. Add margins
items.detail: Leave an even border so nothing important sits near the edge.

items.label: 3. Add columns and gutters
items.detail: Pick a column count that suits the format and keep gutters equal.

items.label: 4. Place the hierarchy
items.detail: Give the headline, image and details their spaces on the grid.

items.label: 5. Check the edges
items.detail: Confirm the safe area, and add bleed if the piece will be printed.

cards.question: Why did the phone number get cut off on the customer's banner?
options: The printer used CMYK ink
It was placed too close to the trim edge instead of inside the safe area
The font was a sans-serif
The banner had too much white space
cards.explanation: Trimming can move slightly. Important content belongs inside the safe area, away from the trim line, and the background should extend into the bleed.

cards.title: Three formats, three ways of looking
cards.body:
Each format is seen in a different way, so the layout must change:

- **Social posts:** seen on a phone while scrolling, for a second or two. One idea, large text, strong contrast. Common shapes are square and tall portrait, but recommended sizes change, so check each platform's current guidance.
- **Banners and signs:** seen from a distance, often while walking or driving. Very few words, huge letters, a logo and one clear action.
- **Print pieces such as flyers and menus:** held in the hand and read up close. More detail is fine, but it still needs a grid, clear groups and margins.

Design the idea once, then rebuild the layout for each format instead of just stretching it.

cards.back: Extra background that extends past the trim line so no white edge shows after cutting. Printers often ask for about 3 mm; always check.
Where the paper will be cut to its final size.
The inner zone where text, logos and key details must stay.
The shape of a design, written as width to height, such as 1:1 for a square.
How much image detail there is. For print, about 300 pixels per inch at final size is a common guide.
The tiny square of colour that makes up a screen image or a raster file.

cards.title: Designing for screen and for print
cards.caption: Set these up at the start. Fixing them at the end takes longer.

items.label: Units
items.right: Millimetres or inches

items.label: Colour mode
items.right: Usually CMYK; ask the printer

items.label: Resolution
items.left: Set by the pixel size of the canvas
items.right: About 300 ppi at final size is a common guide

items.label: Edges
items.left: Keep clear of app buttons and captions
items.right: Add bleed and keep a safe area

items.label: Typical file
items.right: A print-ready PDF

cards.title: Forty words on a shop banner
cards.situation: A fictional hardware store in Faisalabad wants a large banner above the shop. The owner sends forty words: every product, two phone numbers, an email, opening hours and a slogan. People will see it from across a busy road.

choices.text: Suggest the shop name, one main message such as 'Paint, tools and plumbing', and one phone number, in very large letters on a clear grid.
choices.outcome: The owner agrees after Danish shows a quick mock-up from across the room. People can read the banner from the road, and the full list goes on a flyer at the counter.

choices.text: Keep about twenty words but use a condensed font to fit them.
choices.outcome: Better than forty words, but still too much to read from a moving car. A partial fix.

choices.text: Fit all forty words by making the text small.
choices.outcome: From the road, the banner looks like a grey blur. A banner must be readable from a distance or it does not do its job.

cards.title: Which format fits?
cards.prompt: Sort each layout choice under the format it suits best.

items.text: One bold idea readable in two seconds on a phone
Huge letters readable from across a road
A short list of prices, read up close
Key text kept clear of app buttons and captions
Five words or fewer, plus the shop name
Bleed added and text inside the safe area
A tall portrait shape for a phone feed
A map and address on the back side

cards.title: Numbers worth knowing
cards.caption: Common guides. Always confirm sizes and settings with the printer or the platform.

items.label: A4 paper
items.detail: Common for flyers, notices and menus.

items.label: A5 paper
items.detail: Half of A4, popular for handouts.

items.label: Bleed
items.detail: A common request on each edge; some printers ask for more.

items.label: Print resolution
items.detail: A common guide for images at final printed size.

items.label: Square post
items.detail: Width equals height.

cards.question: Danish sets up an A5 flyer for print. Which setup is correct?
options: RGB, 72 pixels wide, no bleed
148 × 210 mm with bleed added and text inside the safe area
A square 1:1 canvas in pixels
Any size, because the printer will stretch it
cards.explanation: A5 is 148 × 210 mm. A print file should be set at the final size, with bleed and a safe area, in the colour mode the printer asks for.

cards.title: One idea, four formats
cards.body:
Rabia is opening a fictional café, Saffron Cup, in Islamabad. Mahnoor plans one idea, 'Grand opening, free chai on Friday', and rebuilds it four times:

- **Square post:** a cup photo on the top two thirds, the headline in large type below, the logo small in a corner.
- **Tall story:** the same parts stacked, with text kept away from the top and bottom where app buttons appear.
- **A5 flyer:** a three-column grid with the menu highlights, map and timings, plus bleed.
- **Shop banner:** only the logo, 'Now open' and 'Free chai Friday'.

The fonts, colours and photo repeat, so all four feel like one campaign.

cards.title: Use natural reading paths
cards.body: In left-to-right languages, people often scan a simple poster in a **Z shape**: top left, across, diagonally down, then across the bottom. Put the headline on top and the action at the bottom right. For text-heavy pages, readers often scan down the left side. The **rule of thirds** helps too: place key items where lines dividing the page into thirds cross. For Urdu layouts, remember the eye starts on the right.

cards.title: Preparing a print-ready file
cards.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order before sending a flyer to the printer.
steps: Ask the printer for size, bleed, colour mode and file format
Set up the document at the final size with bleed and margins
Place images at a high enough resolution for the printed size
Proofread all text, numbers and contact details
Export a print-ready PDF with bleed included
Approve a test print or digital proof before the full run

cards.title: Remember from The Grid Room
items: Build every layout on a grid of margins, columns and gutters.
Keep important content inside the safe area; add bleed for print.
Screens use pixels and RGB; print uses real sizes, usually CMYK and high resolution.
Social posts, banners and flyers are seen differently, so rebuild the layout for each.
Banners need very few words and very large letters.
Ask the printer or check the platform for current sizes and settings.

cards.prompt: Take one message for a business you know and sketch it three ways: a square post, a shop banner and an A5 flyer. Note what you keep, what you cut and where the grid lines fall.

quiz.question: What is a gutter in a layout grid?
options: The empty border around the page
The gap between two columns
The area beyond the trim line
The darkest colour in the palette
quiz.explanation: Gutters are the gaps between columns. Margins are the borders around the page edge.

quiz.question: What is bleed in a print file?
options: Background extended past the trim line
Ink that spreads on cheap paper
A red colour used for sale posters
The space between two lines of text, measured in points
quiz.explanation: Bleed is extra background beyond the trim. If the cut moves slightly, no white edge shows.

quiz.question: Where should a logo and phone number be placed on a printed flyer?
options: Exactly on the trim line
Inside the bleed area
Inside the safe area, away from the trim
Anywhere, because modern printing machines never move or cut unevenly
quiz.explanation: Important content must stay inside the safe area, because trimming can shift slightly.

quiz.question: Which is a common resolution guide for images in print at their final size?
options: 10 pixels per inch
About 300 pixels per inch
Exactly 1 pixel per millimetre
Resolution does not matter in print
quiz.explanation: About 300 ppi at the final printed size is a common guide. Check what your printer recommends for the job.

quiz.question: What are the measurements of A4 paper?
quiz.explanation: A4 is 210 × 297 mm. A5 is half of that, at 148 × 210 mm.

quiz.question: A shop wants forty words on a banner that people see from across a road. What is the best advice?
options: Very few words in very large letters
Use a smaller, condensed font so that all forty words fit on the banner
Use a script font to make it look special
Add more photos to fill the banner
quiz.explanation: Banners are read from a distance and in passing, so they need few words and big letters.

quiz.question: Why should you not simply stretch a square post to make a tall story or a wide banner?
options: Stretching changes the colour mode from RGB to CMYK without warning you
Stretching always deletes the text
Each format is seen differently and stretching distorts it
Apps do not allow different sizes
quiz.explanation: Each format has its own viewing situation. Rebuild the layout for each format and keep the same colours, fonts and idea.

quiz.question: What does an aspect ratio of 1:1 mean?
options: The width and height are equal
The design has one colour
The file is one megabyte
The text is the same size as the image
quiz.explanation: Aspect ratio compares width to height. 1:1 is a square.

quiz.question: On a tall phone story, why keep text away from the very top and bottom?
options: Phones cannot show colour there
Those areas are always cut off when the story is shared to other apps
Grids do not allow text there
App buttons and captions may cover them
quiz.explanation: Many apps show buttons and labels over parts of the screen. Keep key content in the safe middle area and check the platform's current guidance.

quiz.question: What should you do first before preparing a flyer for a new printer?
options: Export a JPG and hope it works
Ask about size, bleed, colour mode and file format
Design in RGB, export a JPG and let the printer convert everything later
Use the smallest file size possible
quiz.explanation: Printers have different requirements. Asking first avoids reprints and wasted money.

sessions.title: Logos and Simple Brand Identity
sessions.summary: Design a logo the way professionals do: start from a brief, sketch many ideas, build the final in vector, test it at small sizes and in one colour, and create logo versions and a one-page brand guide so the brand looks the same everywhere.
objectives: Explain what makes a logo simple, memorable, scalable and original
Tell raster and vector files apart and choose vector for logos
Plan a logo from brief to sketches to final vector artwork
Create logo versions for different backgrounds, shapes and sizes
Write a one-page brand guide with logo rules, colours and fonts

cards.title: Make it like the famous one
cards.setting: A video call between Mahnoor in Karachi and Rabia in Islamabad, with Nida listening in.

lines.text: Page five. Mahnoor has her first real brand client: Rabia, who is opening Saffron Cup café in Islamabad.
Mahnoor, I love this famous coffee brand's logo. Can you make mine just like it, but with my café's name?
Hmm. I could change the colours a little...
Careful. Copying a famous logo, even with changes, can confuse customers and may break trademark and copyright rules. And it will never feel like Rabia's own café.
Oh, I did not think of that. I just want people to feel it is a quality place.
That is the real brief: quality, warmth and something special about Saffron Cup. Let us find out what makes it unique and design from there.
So I start with questions, not with the app. Got it!

scenes.heading: The brief
scenes.narration: Ask about the business, its customers, its values and its competitors. A logo solves a problem: being recognised and remembered.

scenes.heading: Research
scenes.narration: Look at what others in the same field do, so your design stands apart instead of looking like everyone else.

scenes.heading: Sketching
scenes.narration: Draw many quick ideas on paper. Most will be bad, and that is the point. The good ones appear after the obvious ones.

scenes.heading: Vector artwork
scenes.narration: Rebuild the best two or three ideas as vector shapes in a vector editor such as Inkscape, Figma or Adobe Illustrator.

scenes.heading: Testing
scenes.narration: Test each logo very small, very large, in one colour, on dark and light backgrounds. Simple logos survive every test.

scenes.heading: Delivery
scenes.narration: Hand over the final logo versions in the right file formats, with a short brand guide that explains how to use them.

cards.title: A small logo project
cards.caption: A fictional timeline. Agree your own dates with each client.

items.label: Day 1
items.detail: Brief meeting and written summary of what the client needs.

items.label: Days 2–3
items.detail: Research and many rough sketches.

items.label: Days 4–5
items.detail: Two or three ideas built in vector and shown to the client.

items.label: Days 6–8
items.detail: Agreed revision rounds on the chosen idea.

items.label: Days 9–10
items.detail: Final versions, files and a one-page brand guide delivered.

cards.question: Rabia asks for a copy of a famous brand's logo with her café's name. What should Mahnoor do?
options: Copy it but change the colours so it looks different
Explain the risks kindly and design an original logo from a proper brief
Trace the famous logo in a vector app
Use the famous logo as it is, since it is only a small café
cards.explanation: Copying a well-known logo can confuse customers and risk legal problems. An original logo based on the client's own story serves them far better.

cards.title: What makes a good logo
cards.body:
A strong logo is usually:

- **Simple:** easy to recognise at a glance, with few details.
- **Memorable:** one clear idea that people can recall.
- **Scalable:** clear on a tiny profile picture and on a large shop sign.
- **Works in one colour:** it still reads in plain black or plain white, for stamps, receipts or embroidery.
- **Fits the brand:** a children's school and a law firm need different feelings.
- **Original:** not copied or traced from another logo or from stock art.

A logo does not need to show everything the business does. A café logo does not need a cup, a cake, a sandwich and a sofa.

cards.back: The business name in a styled font, with no symbol.
Initials or a single letter, useful for long names.
A simple picture of a real object, such as a leaf or a cup.
A shape that does not show a real object but suggests a feeling.
Text inside a badge or seal shape. It can be hard to read very small.
A symbol and a wordmark together, which can also be used separately.

cards.title: Raster and vector
cards.caption: Logos are built in vector, so they stay sharp at any size.

items.label: Made of
items.right: Shapes defined by points, lines and curves

items.label: Enlarging
items.right: Stays sharp at any size

items.label: Best for
items.right: Logos, icons and illustrations with clean shapes

items.label: Example editors
items.right: Inkscape, Figma, Adobe Illustrator

items.label: Common files
items.right: SVG, PDF, EPS, AI

cards.title: A logo full of details
cards.situation: Mahnoor's first logo idea for Saffron Cup shows a teacup, steam shaped like saffron threads, a crescent, two leaves, the café's full name and 'Since 2026' in a circle. It looks lovely large, but at profile-picture size it becomes a brown blob.

choices.text: Simplify to one strong idea, such as a cup with a single saffron-thread steam line, and test it small and in one colour.
choices.outcome: The new mark is clear even as a tiny icon, and works in black for stamps and in white on the café's dark sign. Rabia recognises it instantly.

choices.text: Keep the detailed logo for big uses and make a separate, simpler icon for small uses.
choices.outcome: Having a small version is a good idea, but if the main logo is too complex it will still struggle on menus, cups and print. A partial fix.

choices.text: Keep it as it is; people will zoom in if they want to see it.
choices.outcome: People do not zoom in on logos. A logo that fails at small sizes fails on phones, where most people will first see it.

cards.title: Pass or fail the logo test?
cards.prompt: Sort each logo feature by whether it helps or hurts a logo.

items.text: Still readable when shown as a tiny icon
Depends on a photo to make sense
Works in plain black and in plain white
Uses six colours and gradients that cannot be printed in one colour
Built from vector shapes
Traced from another company's logo
One clear idea linked to the business
Uses a font whose licence does not allow logo use

cards.title: Layers of a brand identity
cards.caption: A logo is only the visible tip. The deeper layers guide every design choice.

items.label: Everyday materials
items.detail: Menus, posts, cups, signs and uniforms that use the rules.

items.label: Visual style
items.detail: Colours, fonts, photo style and icon style.

items.label: Logo and name
items.detail: The mark people recognise and remember.

items.label: Personality and voice
items.detail: How the brand feels and speaks, such as warm and welcoming.

items.label: Purpose and customers
items.detail: Why the business exists and who it serves.

cards.question: Rabia's café sign is dark brown. Which logo version should Mahnoor provide for it?
options: Only the full-colour version on a white box
A low-resolution JPG of the logo
A reversed version in white or a light colour
A screenshot of the logo from a phone
cards.explanation: A reversed (light) version is designed for dark backgrounds. Good logo packages include versions for light and dark backgrounds.

cards.title: Logo versions and their uses
cards.prompt: Match each logo version with where it is most useful.

pairs.right: Main uses on light backgrounds, such as menus and the website
Dark backgrounds, such as the café's dark brown sign
Stamps, receipts and single-colour printing
Profile pictures, app icons and very small spaces
Wide spaces, such as website headers and shop banners

cards.title: Saffron Cup's one-page brand guide
cards.body:
Mahnoor gives Rabia a single PDF page:

- **Logo:** primary, horizontal, icon only, black and white versions, with a rule to keep clear space around the logo equal to the height of the cup.
- **Do not:** stretch, rotate, recolour or add shadows to the logo.
- **Colours:** saffron orange, deep brown and cream, each with HEX codes for screens and CMYK values for print.
- **Fonts:** one heading font and one body font, both licensed for commercial use, plus a matching Urdu font.
- **Photo style:** warm light, real customers with permission, no heavy filters.
- **Voice:** warm, short and welcoming.

cards.title: Prepare logo files properly
cards.body: Keep an editable master file and give clients final files for each use: vector files (such as SVG, PDF or EPS) for printers and sign makers, and PNG files with transparent backgrounds for screens. In the final vector logo, designers often convert text to outlines (paths), so the logo looks right even on computers without the font. Keep the editable version with live text for future changes. Check that any font used in a logo has a licence that allows logo use.

cards.title: Remember from The Brand Studio
items: Start a logo from a brief and many sketches, not from the app or a famous logo.
Good logos are simple, memorable, scalable, work in one colour and are original.
Build logos in vector so they stay sharp at every size.
Provide versions: primary, horizontal, icon, one-colour and reversed.
A one-page brand guide keeps logo use, colours, fonts and style consistent.
Check font and image licences before using them in a logo.

cards.prompt: Write a five-question brief you would ask a new logo client. Then sketch three very different logo ideas for a fictional business and say which one passes the small-size and one-colour tests.

quiz.question: Why are logos usually built as vector files?
options: Vectors stay sharp at any size
Vectors have more colours than raster files
Vectors cannot be edited later
Vectors only work on screens
quiz.explanation: Vector shapes are drawn from points and curves, so they can scale from a stamp to a billboard without blurring.

quiz.question: What is a wordmark?
options: A logo that is only a picture
Text inside a badge shape
The business name set in a styled font, with no symbol
A watermark on a draft
quiz.explanation: A wordmark is a logo made from the name itself, styled in a particular way.

quiz.question: What is the best first step in a logo project?
options: Choosing colours
Opening a vector editor and drawing the first shapes that come to mind
Searching for a logo to copy
Understanding the business through a brief
quiz.explanation: A brief explains the business, customers and values, which tell you what the logo must communicate.

quiz.question: Which test checks whether a logo is simple enough?
options: Printing it on the largest possible banner
Viewing it as a tiny icon and in one colour
Adding a gradient to it
Showing it only on a white background
quiz.explanation: Small sizes and single-colour use reveal too much detail. Simple logos pass both tests.

quiz.question: A café sign has a dark background. Which logo version suits it?
options: A reversed version in white or a light colour
The full-colour version meant for light backgrounds
A low-resolution JPG
A version with extra shadows
quiz.explanation: Reversed versions are made for dark backgrounds, so the logo stays visible and on-brand.

quiz.question: Which of these belongs in a simple brand guide?
options: The client's bank account details
Logo versions, clear space, colours and fonts
Every draft the designer rejected
The designer's personal social media passwords and login details
quiz.explanation: A brand guide shows how to use the logo, colours, fonts and style consistently.

quiz.question: A client asks you to copy a famous company's logo with small changes. What is the main problem?
options: It takes too long to trace
Famous logos are always vector files, so they cannot be edited in any normal app
It may confuse customers and break trademark rules
Famous logos only work in English
quiz.explanation: Copying a known logo can mislead customers and create legal risk, and it gives the client no identity of their own.

quiz.question: Why might a designer convert logo text to outlines in the final vector file?
options: To make the file use more colours
To make the text easy for anyone to edit and change later on any computer
To change the font licence
So it displays correctly without the font
quiz.explanation: Outlined text becomes shapes, so it displays correctly anywhere. Keep an editable master with live text too.

quiz.question: Which file is usually best for a sign maker who needs to enlarge a logo?
options: A small PNG copied from a website
A vector file such as SVG, PDF or EPS
A phone screenshot
A JPG saved at low quality
quiz.explanation: Vector files scale without losing quality, which sign makers and printers need.

quiz.question: Which describes a combination mark?
options: A symbol and a wordmark used together
Only the initials of a business
A logo made from a photo
A logo that changes its colours every month to match the seasons
quiz.explanation: A combination mark pairs a symbol with the name. Each part can often be used on its own when space is limited.

sessions.title: Working with Clients and Building a Portfolio
sessions.summary: Turn skills into paid work. Write and use a clear brief, manage revisions, deliver the right file formats and sizes, respect copyright and licences for fonts and images, build a portfolio of case studies, set your own prices with a simple method and avoid common scams.
objectives: Run a design project from brief to final handover
Agree scope, revision rounds, timelines and payment in writing
Deliver correct file formats and export sizes for each use
Check copyright and licences for fonts, photos and graphics
Build a portfolio of case studies and price your work with a clear method

cards.title: The eleventh revision
cards.setting: A group call. Mahnoor is in Karachi, Danish in Peshawar and Nida in Lahore.

lines.text: The last page of the sketchbook. Mahnoor and Danish are ready to work as designers, but business brings new problems.
A client asked for 'a small poster'. I am now on revision eleven. Every time he wants something new. And I have not been paid anything yet!
And someone messaged me offering a big design job if I first pay a registration fee. Is that normal?
No to both. A real client does not ask you to pay to get work. And endless revisions happen when nothing was agreed in writing.
Professionals use a brief, a short agreement, a set number of revision rounds and an advance payment. It protects both sides.
Rabia's café project went well because we wrote everything down first. Can I show it in my portfolio?
Ask Rabia's permission, then turn it into a case study. That is how your next client will find you.

cards.title: A professional project, start to finish

scenes.heading: Brief
scenes.narration: Collect what the client needs: goal, audience, message, sizes, deadline, budget range and examples they like or dislike.

scenes.heading: Proposal
scenes.narration: Send a short written proposal: what is included, revision rounds, timeline, price and payment terms.

scenes.heading: Advance
scenes.narration: Many designers ask for part of the fee before starting. It shows the client is serious.

scenes.heading: Concepts and revisions
scenes.narration: Share drafts, collect feedback in one clear list per round, and stay within the agreed rounds.

scenes.heading: Handover
scenes.narration: After final payment, deliver the agreed files in the right formats and sizes, with a note on how to use them.

cards.title: The project flow
cards.caption: Write each step down. Clear steps prevent most client problems.

items.label: 1. Brief
items.detail: Understand the goal, audience and deliverables.

items.label: 2. Written agreement
items.detail: Scope, rounds, dates, price, payment and rights.

items.label: 3. Advance payment
items.detail: Received before the main work begins.

items.label: 4. Drafts and agreed revisions
items.detail: Feedback collected in one list per round.

items.label: 5. Final payment and files
items.detail: Agreed formats delivered and the project closed.

cards.question: Danish is on revision eleven of a 'small poster' with no payment. What would have prevented this?
options: Working faster on each revision
Using more colours in the first draft
A written agreement with scope, revision rounds and an advance payment
Sending files without a watermark
cards.explanation: Agreeing scope and the number of revision rounds in writing, with an advance, sets clear limits. Extra rounds can then be charged at an agreed rate.

cards.title: Questions for a good brief
cards.body:
A brief is a short document that explains the job. Ask:

- **Goal:** what should this design achieve? More orders, event sign-ups, awareness?
- **Audience:** who will see it, and where: phone, shop wall, newspaper?
- **Message:** the one main thing people must understand.
- **Deliverables:** which pieces, sizes and formats are needed?
- **Content:** who supplies the text, photos and logo, and are they cleared for use?
- **Brand:** existing colours, fonts or guide.
- **Deadline and budget range.**
- **Likes and dislikes:** examples they like, and why.

Send a short summary back and ask the client to confirm it. That summary becomes your checklist.

cards.title: Files for the job
cards.prompt: Match each file format with its usual best use. Exact needs vary, so ask each client or printer.

pairs.right: Photos and social posts where a small file size helps
Graphics and logos that need a transparent background on screen
Vector logos and icons for websites and digital use
Print-ready files and documents to share with layout intact
Future edits, shared only if the agreement includes it

cards.title: Two ways to price your work
cards.caption: Pick the method that suits the job. Do not copy other people's rates; work out your own.

items.label: How it works
items.left: You charge for the time you spend
items.right: You agree one price for a defined set of work

items.label: Good for
items.right: Logos, posters and packages with a clear scope

items.label: Client feels
items.right: Knows the cost in advance

items.label: Your risk
items.left: Lower if hours are tracked honestly
items.right: Higher if scope or rounds are not written down

items.label: Key habit
items.right: List exactly what is included

cards.title: The registration fee
cards.situation: Mahnoor gets a message from an unknown account: 'We are a big company. We will give you 50 design jobs. To join our team, pay a small registration fee today. Also, please send us a sample logo for our main brand, unpaid, as a test.'

choices.text: Decline politely, do not pay, and do not create free full logos; offer to share your portfolio and work only through a written, paid agreement.
choices.outcome: The account goes silent. Mahnoor loses nothing. Real clients pay designers; they do not charge designers for jobs or demand full unpaid work.

choices.text: Do not pay the fee, but create the free test logo to see if they are real.
choices.outcome: She avoids losing money, but her free logo could be used without payment. A small, clearly limited test is sometimes fine; a full brand logo is not.

choices.text: Pay the fee because fifty jobs would be worth it.
choices.outcome: This is a common pattern used in scams aimed at freelancers. The fee is gone and no jobs arrive. Never pay to receive work.

cards.title: Can you use it?
cards.prompt: Sort each image or font situation into the safest action.

items.text: Your own photo of a product you were hired to promote
A photo from a free stock website for a client's paid advert
An image copied from a web search result
A font labelled 'free for personal use' in a client's logo
A famous cartoon character on a shop's poster without permission
Graphics you drew yourself from scratch
A Creative Commons image with attribution conditions
Another designer's portfolio piece presented as your own

cards.title: From viewer to client
cards.caption: A good portfolio moves people step by step towards working with you.

items.label: Sees your work
items.detail: On your portfolio site, social pages or a freelancing profile.

items.label: Reads a case study
items.detail: Understands the problem you solved and how.

items.label: Trusts you
items.detail: Sees clear process, honest results and client permission.

items.label: Contacts you
items.detail: Finds a clear way to reach you and what you offer.

items.label: Becomes a client
items.detail: Agrees a brief and a written proposal.

cards.question: Mahnoor wants to use a font marked 'free for personal use' in Rabia's café logo. What should she do?
options: Use it, since free fonts can be used for anything
Read the licence and get a commercial licence, or choose a font licensed for commercial and logo use
Use it and change the name of the font
Use it only in the black version of the logo
cards.explanation: 'Personal use' licences usually do not cover business use. A logo is commercial, so the font's licence must allow that use.

cards.title: Mahnoor's case study page
cards.body:
With Rabia's written permission, Mahnoor adds one case study to her portfolio:

- **The challenge:** a new café in Islamabad needed an identity that felt warm and special, not like a copy of big chains.
- **The process:** brief, research of other cafés, twenty sketches, three vector ideas, two revision rounds.
- **The solution:** a cup icon with a saffron-thread steam line, a brand guide, opening posts, an A5 flyer and a shop banner.
- **The result, honestly stated:** Rabia's comment that customers mention the logo, with no invented numbers.

She shows five strong projects instead of thirty weak ones, including two self-initiated practice projects labelled as such.

cards.title: Warning signs of a scam
Setting your own price
cards.prompt: Put these steps in a sensible order when pricing a new project.
steps: List exactly what is included: pieces, sizes, formats and revision rounds
Estimate the hours for briefing, design, revisions and file preparation
Decide the income you need per hour to cover your costs and time
Adjust for the value and use of the work, such as a logo used for years
Write the price, advance and payment dates in a short proposal

cards.back: The exact list of work included in the price.
One agreed set of changes, collected from the client in a single list.
The final files the client receives, with formats and sizes.
How and where the client may use the designs, agreed in writing.
The editable working files. Whether they are handed over should be agreed in advance.
Permission for the designer to show the work, sometimes after a launch date.

cards.title: Remember from The Open Portfolio
items: Every project starts with a brief confirmed by the client in writing.
Agree scope, revision rounds, dates, payment and rights before starting.
Deliver the right formats for each use and ask printers and clients what they need.
Use only fonts and images you have the right to use; check each licence.
Show a few strong case studies, with client permission and honest results.
Price with your own clear method, and never pay a fee to get work.

cards.prompt: Write a one-paragraph design package you could offer: what is included, how many revision rounds, the timeline and what you need from the client. Then list three things you will check before using any font or photo.

quiz.question: What is a design brief?
options: A short summary of the job and its goals
The final invoice
A list of every font and colour installed on your computer
A type of logo
quiz.explanation: A brief sets out what the job is. It guides the design and becomes a checklist for approval.

quiz.question: Why agree the number of revision rounds in writing?
options: So the client cannot give any feedback
To set clear limits, so extra rounds can be discussed and charged fairly
Because apps limit how many times a file can be saved
To avoid sending drafts
quiz.explanation: Written rounds protect both sides. The client knows what is included, and the designer avoids endless unpaid changes.

quiz.question: Which file format usually suits a logo that needs a transparent background on a website?
options: JPG
A phone screenshot
