PNG or SVG
A Word document
quiz.explanation: PNG supports transparency for raster images, and SVG is a vector format for the web. JPG does not support transparency.

quiz.question: A font is labelled 'free for personal use'. Can you use it in a client's paid advert?
options: Yes, free fonts can be used anywhere, for any purpose, by anyone
Yes, if you change the colour
Only if the advert is printed
Not without checking the licence first
quiz.explanation: Personal-use licences usually do not cover commercial work. Get the right licence or choose another font.

quiz.question: Someone offers you many design jobs if you first pay a registration fee. What is this most likely to be?
options: A common scam pattern aimed at freelancers
A normal hiring step
A tax requirement
A portfolio review
quiz.explanation: Real clients pay designers. Being asked to pay to receive work is a well-known warning sign.

quiz.question: What makes a strong portfolio case study?
options: As many projects as possible, including weak early ones, to show volume
Challenge, process, solution and honest result
Only the final logo with no explanation
Invented sales figures to impress clients
quiz.explanation: Case studies show how you think. Results must be honest, and client work should be shown with permission.

quiz.question: Which is the safest way to find a photo for a client's advert?
options: Copy one from a web search result
Take a screenshot from a competitor's page and crop it so it looks different
Use another designer's portfolio image
Use your own photo or a properly licensed one
quiz.explanation: Images found in search results are usually owned by someone. Use your own photos or properly licensed ones and keep a record.

quiz.question: When is charging per project usually a good choice?
options: When the scope is clear and written down
When the client cannot describe the work at all and expects you to guess
When you want to avoid writing anything down
When the work is endless small edits
quiz.explanation: Project pricing works when exactly what is included is written down. Unclear or ongoing work often suits hourly pricing.

quiz.question: What is a sensible first step when setting your own price for a project?
options: Copy the lowest price you can find online
Ask the client to choose any price
List exactly what is included, then estimate the hours it needs
Charge the same for every project
quiz.explanation: Pricing starts with the scope. Then estimate time, decide your hourly need and adjust for the value of the work.

quiz.question: Should editable source files always be handed to the client?
options: Yes, always, without discussion
Never, under any circumstances
Only if they are smaller than the final files
It depends on what was agreed in writing at the start
quiz.explanation: Handing over source files is a choice that should be agreed in advance, and it may affect the price.

bank.question: A flyer has a large headline, a large photo and a large offer, all bold and orange. The squint test shows no clear focus. What is the best next step?
options: Add an orange border around all three
Choose one winner and tone down the rest
Make all three larger until they touch and fill the whole page
Change the background to orange as well
bank.explanation: Hierarchy needs one clear winner. Reducing the emphasis on supporting items lets the main message lead.

bank.question: On a price list, each item's price sits far away in a separate block at the bottom. Which principle is mainly broken?
options: Repetition
Contrast
Proximity
Alignment
bank.explanation: Related items, such as an item and its price, should sit close together. Proximity groups them into one unit.

bank.question: A booklet's pages each use different heading fonts, colours and icon styles, so it feels like five different documents. What fixes this most directly?
options: Repeating the same fonts, colours and icon style on every page
Adding more white space only on the cover
Centring all the text
Using a bigger headline on page one
bank.explanation: Repetition ties pages together. Consistent fonts, colours and shapes make a set feel like one family.

bank.question: Which statement about white space is most accurate?
options: It should be filled with small details so no space is wasted
It only refers to areas that are coloured white
It is mainly a way to save printing ink
It separates groups and draws attention to what matters
bank.explanation: White space, also called negative space, can be any colour. It separates groups and focuses attention.

bank.question: A design is neat and well aligned, but viewers say it is 'boring' and they do not notice the offer. Which change helps most?
options: Break the alignment on purpose so that the page looks more lively
Add contrast to the offer
Add three more photos
Reduce the white space
bank.explanation: The structure is fine; the problem is weak contrast. Make the key message clearly different so it stands out.

bank.question: Mahnoor's text boxes are centred, left-aligned and right-aligned at random. She wants the page to look planned. What should she do?
options: Use a different font in each box
Make each box a different colour
Choose one clear alignment and line items up along it
Add more space only around the logo
bank.explanation: Mixed alignment looks accidental. Choosing one alignment system creates visible order.

bank.question: Why do designers plan the reading order on paper before opening any app?
options: Apps cannot show hierarchy
Paper sketches print better
Clients usually ask to see paper drafts before any digital work starts
It sets what matters before any styling
bank.explanation: Planning the order of importance first gives every later choice, from size to colour, a clear purpose.

bank.question: A designer wants a calm, natural palette for a plant nursery using colours side by side on the colour wheel. What kind of scheme is this?
options: Complementary
Analogous
Triadic
Reversed
bank.explanation: Analogous colours are neighbours on the wheel, such as yellow-green, green and blue-green, and they feel calm together.

bank.question: Body text measures 3.2:1 against its background in a contrast checker. Under the common WCAG AA guide, which statement is correct?
options: It passes for all text sizes
It fails for normal body text
It fails only for print
It passes, because 3:1 is the highest ratio checkers measure
bank.explanation: WCAG AA asks for 4.5:1 for normal text. 3:1 is the minimum only for large text.

bank.question: A client's flyer was designed in RGB with a very bright neon green, and the printed result looks dull. What is the most professional way to avoid this next time?
options: Increase the screen brightness before sending
Use only black and white for all print jobs
Save the file as a PNG instead
Prepare the file for the printer's colour needs and ask for a test print of key colours
bank.explanation: Some bright RGB colours cannot be matched with ink. Working with the printer's settings and checking a proof avoids surprises.

bank.question: In the 60-30-10 guideline, a designer uses the accent colour for the background, headings, icons and buttons. What is the main problem?
options: The accent no longer stands out
Accent colours cannot be shown on screens, only printed on paper
The design now has too few colours
Headings must always be black
bank.explanation: An accent works because it is rare. Spread everywhere, it stops guiding the eye.

bank.question: Which pair is complementary on the basic colour wheel?
options: Red and orange
Blue and violet
Red and green
Yellow and orange
bank.explanation: Red and green sit opposite each other, so they are complementary. The other pairs are neighbours.

bank.question: A map uses only red and green dots to show 'open' and 'closed' shops. What is the best improvement?
options: Make the red brighter
Add labels or shapes as well as colour
Use a lighter green
Remove the legend to save space and make the dots a little larger
bank.explanation: People with colour vision deficiency may not tell red from green. Shapes or labels make the meaning clear to everyone.

bank.question: What happens when you mix more ink in CMYK printing, compared with adding more light in RGB?
options: Both become lighter
Both become darker
More light makes colours darker; more ink makes colours lighter
More light: brighter. More ink: darker
bank.explanation: RGB adds light, moving towards white. CMYK adds ink, which absorbs light and moves towards dark.

bank.question: A designer pairs two sans-serif fonts that look almost the same for headings and body text. What is the likely result?
options: Strong, clear contrast
It looks like a mistake, not a choice
Better Urdu support
A smaller file size that prints faster and costs less at the press
bank.explanation: Pairs need clear contrast. Nearly identical fonts look accidental; use a clear contrast or one family in different weights.

bank.question: A headline is too wide for its box. Which fix keeps the letters looking professional?
options: Squash the text horizontally to fit
Stretch the box and the text together
Reduce the size, rewrite it shorter or change the layout
Convert it to a low-resolution image
bank.explanation: Stretching or squashing distorts letter shapes. Change size, wording or layout instead.

bank.question: Nastaliq Urdu lines on a poster overlap each other. Which setting should be adjusted first?
options: Line spacing (leading)
Kerning between two English letters
The colour mode
The bleed
bank.explanation: Nastaliq letters rise and fall at angles, so they need extra line spacing to stop lines touching.

bank.question: In a design app, Urdu text shows as separate letters in reversed order. What is the best first action?
options: Take a phone screenshot of correct Urdu and paste it
Type each letter backwards by hand
Make the text larger
Use a font and app that properly support Urdu, then check with a native reader
bank.explanation: Broken or reversed Urdu usually means missing support for right-to-left shaping. A supported font and app fix the cause.

bank.question: What is the difference between kerning and tracking?
options: Kerning changes the line spacing, while tracking changes the font weight of a word
Kerning: one letter pair; tracking: a whole word or line
They are two names for the same setting
Kerning is for Urdu only; tracking is for English only
bank.explanation: Kerning fixes the gap between a particular pair of letters. Tracking changes spacing evenly across many letters.

bank.question: A school wants its rules for parents in a decorative script font, all in capitals. What advice is best?
options: Agree, because script fonts look friendly
Use script only for the title, and set the rules in a plain font in normal sentence case
Make the script font smaller so more fits
Use three script fonts for variety
bank.explanation: Long text in script or all capitals is hard to read. Keep decorative fonts for a few words and use plain fonts for reading.

bank.question: On a bilingual banner, the Urdu text looks much smaller than the English even at the same point size. What should the designer do?
options: Leave it, because sizes are equal in points
Remove the Urdu text
Adjust the Urdu size until both languages look visually equal
Change the English to all capitals
bank.explanation: Different scripts appear different sizes at the same point size. Judge by eye so both languages look equally important.

bank.question: A printer asks for 3 mm bleed on an A5 flyer (148 × 210 mm). What is the full document size including bleed?
bank.explanation: Bleed is added on every edge: 3 mm on each side adds 6 mm to both width and height, giving 154 × 216 mm.

bank.question: A photo is 1,200 pixels wide. At a common print guide of 300 ppi, about how wide can it print while staying sharp?
options: About 4 inches
About 12 inches
About 30 inches
About 1 inch
bank.explanation: 1,200 pixels divided by 300 pixels per inch is about 4 inches.

bank.question: What is the main purpose of a safe area?
options: To mark where bleed is added so the printer knows where to cut
To protect key content near the edges
To store spare colours
To set the colour mode
bank.explanation: The safe area protects important content from trim movement in print and from app buttons on screens.

bank.question: A designer stretches a square post sideways to make a wide website banner. What is the better approach?
options: Stretch it more evenly
Crop out the headline
Rebuild the layout for the wide format, keeping the same idea, colours and fonts
Shrink it and leave empty bars on both sides
bank.explanation: Each format needs its own layout. Rebuilding keeps the hierarchy clear and avoids distortion.

bank.question: On a grid, what are gutters?
options: The gaps between columns
The margins around the page
The lines where paper is cut
The highest-resolution images
bank.explanation: Gutters separate columns. Equal gutters keep a layout tidy.

bank.question: A tall phone story has its key offer at the very bottom edge. Why is this risky?
options: Phones cannot display any text in the bottom tenth of the screen
Bottom areas are printed in CMYK
Grids forbid text in the bottom third
App buttons or captions may cover it
bank.explanation: Platform interfaces overlay parts of the screen. Keep key content in the safe middle and check current guidance.

bank.question: Which reading pattern describes how people often scan a simple poster in a left-to-right language?
options: A circle from the centre outwards
A Z shape from top left to bottom right
Bottom to top
Right to left along the bottom
bank.explanation: People often scan simple layouts in a Z path. Put the headline at the top and the action near the end of the path.

bank.question: A logo looks great on a laptop but becomes a blurry blob when printed on a large shop sign. What is the most likely cause?
options: It was made in vector
A small raster file was enlarged too far
The sign used CMYK ink
The logo had too much white space around it, which printed grey
bank.explanation: Raster images lose quality when enlarged. Logos should be built and supplied in vector.

bank.question: Which logo is most likely to pass the small-size test?
options: A detailed scene with six objects and fine text
A photo of the shop front
A simple shape with one clear idea
A badge with a long slogan in small letters
bank.explanation: Simple marks stay recognisable at tiny sizes. Detail and small text disappear.

bank.question: Why should a logo work in a single colour?
options: Single-colour logos are cheaper to design
Clients prefer black logos
Vector files only support one colour
It is often needed for stamps, receipts, embroidery and one-colour printing
bank.explanation: Many real uses allow only one colour. A logo that relies on colour or gradients fails there.

bank.question: What is the purpose of a clear space rule in a brand guide?
options: Keeps other elements a set distance away
Leaving the logo out of busy designs
Making the logo transparent
Gives the logo a white box behind it at all times, on every background
bank.explanation: Clear space keeps the logo from being crowded by text or images, so it remains clear and consistent.

bank.question: A designer delivers a logo using a font that is licensed only for personal use. What is the risk?
options: The logo will print in the wrong colour
The logo cannot be resized
The client's business use of the logo may break the font licence
The logo will only work in Urdu
bank.explanation: A logo is commercial use. The font's licence must allow logo and commercial use, or the client may face problems.

bank.question: Which set of files best suits a typical small-business logo handover?
options: One JPG on a white background
Vector files for print and signs, transparent PNGs for screens, and light and dark versions
A screenshot of the design app
Only the editable source file
bank.explanation: Different uses need different files. Vector for scaling, PNG with transparency for screens, and versions for backgrounds.

bank.question: Why do designers often sketch many logo ideas before using software?
options: Software cannot draw logos
Clients only accept paper sketches
Sketching is required by printers
Quick sketches explore many ideas fast, and better ideas appear after the obvious ones
bank.explanation: Paper is fast and cheap. Exploring many ideas early leads to stronger, more original solutions.

bank.question: A client sends new feedback every few hours across messages, calls and voice notes. What is the most professional way to manage revisions?
options: Make every change as soon as it arrives, so the client feels heard
One clear feedback list per agreed round
Stop replying until the deadline
Accept only feedback by phone call
bank.explanation: One consolidated list per round keeps changes clear, avoids contradictions and keeps the project within the agreed rounds.

bank.question: A stranger overpays you for a design and asks you to send the extra amount back quickly. What should you suspect?
options: A common overpayment scam
A normal tip
A tax refund
A mistake that you must fix immediately
bank.explanation: Overpayment followed by a refund request is a known scam pattern. The original payment may later be reversed.

bank.question: Mahnoor wants to show Rabia's café project in her portfolio. What should she do first?
options: Post it right away, since she designed it and owns all the work
Change the café's name and post it
Get Rabia's permission first
Wait a year and then post it
bank.explanation: Showing client work should be agreed with the client. A portfolio clause in the agreement makes this clear.

bank.question: A designer is unsure of a fair price and finds another designer's rate card online. What is the better approach?
options: Copy that rate card exactly
Charge as little as possible to win every job
Ask the client to set the price
Work out your own price from scope, hours, costs and the value of the work
bank.explanation: Your own price should reflect your costs, time, skill and the value of the work, not a copied number.

bank.question: A client wants a photo for a paid advert and suggests copying one from a web search. What is the right response?
options: Use it, because search engines make images free
Use it but crop it so it looks different
Explain that it is probably owned by someone and use a licensed or original photo instead
Use it only if the advert is small
bank.explanation: Images in search results usually belong to their creators. Licensed or original photos protect the client.

bank.question: Which brief question most helps a designer decide the size and layout of a design?
options: Where and how will people see it?
What is the client's favourite food?
How many other designers has the client already contacted for quotes?
Which phone does the client use?
bank.explanation: Where a design is seen decides its format, size and how much text it can carry.

bank.question: A portfolio has thirty projects, including weak early pieces and one copied from a tutorial without credit. What is the best improvement?
options: Add ten more projects
Keep only a few strong, original case studies, and label practice projects honestly
Remove all text so the images speak for themselves
Add invented results to every project
bank.explanation: Quality beats quantity. Honest, original case studies build trust; copied or invented content destroys it.
